title: CAPRI: A Context-Aware Privacy Framework for Multi-Agent Generative AI Applications
notes: CAPRI inserts a local 'gatekeeper' LLM between an enterprise and a cloud LLM agent, converting user input into typed entity structures whose PII values are contextually pseudonymized and reversibly mapped via UUIDs before a ReAct agent reasons over them. Its relevance to RQ1 is indirect but structurally analogous: it measures what happens to task completion when an agent is forced to operate over a constrained, structured representation instead of raw natural-language input. The finding is a graded utility cost - imposing entity structure alone improved task success and reduced turns relative to an unconstrained ReAct baseline, whereas heavy pseudonymization degraded success sharply because referential integrity broke inside reasoning traces. For RQ2 it contributes an empirically evaluated control mechanism (local pre-processing gate plus reversible mapping) benchmarked against an unmodified ToolEmu ReAct prompt. The paper reports no compliance or violation metric at all, only task success and turn counts, so it speaks to the 'task completion' side of RQ1 rather than the 'policy violation' side.

quotes.text: The entity-only configuration improved the success rate by 4% and reduced the number of conversational turns by 1.3 compared to the baseline.
As shown in Table 1, this configuration outperformed the fully pseudonymized approach, achieving a 56% success rate while reducing the number of conversational turns by 1.1 compared to the baseline.
Although the integration of entity structures into user queries yielded improvements, the overall success rate for all four (4) configurations remained limited to a maximum of 64%.

extraction.topology: pipeline (local gatekeeper LLM for NER, entity mapping and pseudonymization, feeding a cloud-hosted ReAct tool-using agent)
extraction.benchmark: ToolEmu toolkits, restricted to the Venmo and EpicFHIR toolsets (20 questions over 5 Venmo scenarios; 30 questions over 3 EpicFHIR scenarios)
extraction.baseline: LLM agents running an out-of-the-box ToolEmu ReAct prompt on unmodified tool definitions with no entity structures and no pseudonymization
extraction.key_results: Four configurations compared: entity-only improved success rate by 4% and reduced conversational turns by 1.3 vs baseline; fully pseudonymized reached 42% success with only a 0.38-turn reduction; partially pseudonymized reached 56% success with a 1.1-turn reduction; the maximum success rate across all four configurations was 64%.
extraction.limitations: Authors state that GPT-3.5 Turbo often failed to capture the intended meaning of user queries, capping success at 64% across all configurations, and that more sophisticated models warrant further investigation; the local gatekeeper was a 4-bit quantized Llama 3.1 8B chosen because of limited GPU resources; full pseudonymization introduced referential-integrity failures in reasoning traces.

title: Retail Resilience Engine: An Agentic AI Framework for Building Reliable Retail Systems With Test-Driven Development Approach
notes: This paper proposes the Retail Resilience Engine, a layered agentic-AI framework that fine-tunes a transformer on retail and test-driven-development corpora and wraps it in a keyword-similarity prompt filter plus a test-first validation loop. Its contribution to RQ2 is a control mechanism of a different kind from formal constraints: generated test cases and pass/fail gates used as the reliability mechanism, evaluated against a human-expert baseline rather than against another agent configuration. For RQ1 the evidence is weak - there is no policy, no violation metric and no compliance-critical process; the reported outcome is decision agreement with experts and plan-quality scores. Reported numbers are internally inconsistent (the abstract and conclusion claim a 97.5% similarity index while the body reports a Pearson correlation of 0.96, and filtering accuracy is given as 98.2%, 98.20% and 98.22% in different places), which should be weighed when citing it. Evaluation samples are very small (ten queries for the alignment experiment, ten domains for robustness).

quotes.text: The ρ is 0.96, which means that the decision made by the proposed system is 96% similar to the decision made by human specialists.
The proposed RRE achieved a total score of 13 out of 15, on par with Expert 3 and only slightly below Expert 1.
While the engine performs well across various retail domains, its effectiveness is currently limited to predefined categories such as inventory management and demand forecasting.

extraction.topology: single-agent layered pipeline (data source, pre-processing, feature management, software layer with AI Agent API and Application Control Unit); the paper frames this as replacing multi-level human decision-making with single-point agentic decision-making
extraction.benchmark: No public benchmark; a proprietary corpus of 100,000 documents (5,000 customer reviews, 10,000 inventory records, 50,000 operational-log documents, 35,000 analytics/system-log documents), with 10 retail queries for the alignment experiment, 100/500/1000-query scalability sets, 10 retail domains for robustness, and 5 filtering experiments
extraction.baseline: Human experts with more than 10 years of experience in retail system development, used both for decision-impact ratings and for implementation-plan quality scoring
extraction.key_results: Retail Decision Impact Alignment Pearson correlation rho = 0.96 (abstract and conclusion instead state a 97.5% similarity index); paired t-test p = 0.021 against alpha = 0.05; implementation plan quality 13 out of 15 versus experts; average prompt-filtering accuracy reported as 98.20% (and as 98.22% elsewhere in the text); accuracy above 90% across all ten tested retail domains; 52 ms average inference per query and 4.2 GB memory on an NVIDIA A100.
extraction.limitations: Authors state ethical and data-privacy exposure from PII in training data with no federated learning or differential privacy yet; effectiveness limited to predefined retail categories; the engine operates as a black box with no explainability; real-time scalability requires further optimization; hyperparameters were set heuristically rather than optimized; centralized cloud-only design; decision latency, unpredictable market conditions, and dependence on high-quality input data are named as agentic-AI challenges.

title: Solver-Aided Verification of Policy Compliance in Tool-Augmented LLM Agents
notes: This is the most direct RQ1 test in this batch: the same airline operational policy is given to one agent as a natural-language policy document in context and to another as SMT-LIB-2.0 constraints checked by Z3 as a pre-condition on every planned tool call, with blocked calls returned to the agent alongside a minimum unsatisfiable core for replanning. The result is a precision/recall trade-off rather than a free lunch - invalid write tool calls fell to 29% of write calls while the fraction of correct write calls also fell, yet end-to-end pass^k task success did not degrade and in fact improved slightly and was more consistent across repeated trials. For RQ2 the paper also supplies a rare negative result on the upstream translation step: four successive designs for compiling natural-language policy into logic all failed on syntactic correctness, semantic completeness or constraint tightness until manual review and tuning were added. That makes the reported compliance gain contingent on human-curated encodings rather than on automated policy compilation.

quotes.text: However, prompt-based guidance does not provide reliable policy enforcement. As policies grow longer and more complex, purely prompt-based enforcement becomes increasingly brittle and harder to validate.

While the baseline produced a roughly equal proportion of valid and invalid write tool calls, theTaLLMwith policy checker reduced the fraction of invalid write tool calls to29%(measured over all write tool calls).
Overall, both achieve similar success rates, with the policy checker yielding a slight improvement.

extraction.topology: single-agent tool-planning loop with an external runtime gate that intercepts each candidate tool call, checks it against an SMT policy encoding via Z3, and prompts replanning (bounded to three attempts) on UNSAT
extraction.benchmark: tau2-bench (tau2-verified lineage), airline domain only: 50 tasks, 13 tools, and a 1242-word policy document; 4 trials per task with pass^k reporting; GPT-4.1 as customer and service agent, GPT-4o for tool-call validation
extraction.baseline: The same tool-augmented LLM agent with the natural-language policy document supplied in context and no solver-aided checking (prompt-based policy steering)
extraction.key_results: Invalid write tool calls fell to 29% of all write tool calls under solver-aided checking versus a roughly equal valid/invalid split for the baseline; write-call precision and recall shifted from 0.51/0.61 (baseline) to 0.70/0.49 (solver-aided); pass^1 through pass^4 were 0.560, 0.433, 0.375, 0.340 for the baseline versus 0.625, 0.543, 0.495, 0.460 for the solver-aided agent; success rate decreased by only 26% as k increased versus 40% for the baseline.
extraction.limitations: Authors state that automatically translating natural-language policies into logical constraints is challenging and that verifying semantic completeness requires manual review, so policy encodings are treated as explicit human-reviewed artifacts rather than fully automated output; three recurring failure classes are named (syntactic correctness, semantic completeness, constraint tightness); the solver-aided agent produces fewer correct write tool calls than the baseline; only the airline domain of the benchmark was evaluated; only tool-use policies are covered, excluding behavioural policies such as information-disclosure and confirmation rules.

title: Compliance Digital Twins for Autonomous Financial Agents: Reliability-Aware Scenario Assurance via Calibrated LLM Evaluation
notes: The Compliance Digital Twin proposes a synchronized machine-readable model of financial process graphs, control mappings, segregation-of-duties rules and IAM entitlements, against which agents are exercised on injected routine, degraded and adversarial scenarios before deployment. Two elements matter for RQ1: the explicit process model (process graphs with decision points, handoffs and exception paths) is the normative baseline against which agent behaviour is judged, and a reliability-aware control layer converts an estimated violation risk into a three-level autonomy policy (autonomous, supervised, human-gated) with default thresholds of 0.35 and 0.65. For RQ2 the evaluated control mechanism is pre-deployment scenario assurance plus a calibrated LLM judge, benchmarked against a conventional test suite. The central caveat is that the agents were not real LLM agents: agent behaviour was a probabilistic but scripted decision model, so the reported detection gains are properties of the assurance harness rather than evidence about how LLM agents behave under process constraints. The paper also reports the conventional baseline detection rate as 43% in the text and 47% in the per-family table.

quotes.text: The CDT detected 89% of injected compliance violations and authorization failures before simulated deployment, compared with 43% for the conventional test suite, a 46 percentage -point improvement.
SoD enforcement efficacy reached 96% across the 30 injected toxic entitlement scenarios
These results are reported for a controlled simulation on a single synthetic workflow and should be interpreted as indicative rather than definitive.

extraction.topology: three-agent pipeline (document-interpretation, approval-routing, payment-release) under a reliability-aware supervisory control layer that modulates autonomy between autonomous, supervised and human-gated modes
extraction.benchmark: No public benchmark; a synthetic invoice-to-payment (accounts payable) workflow with 150 parameterized scenario instances across five scenario families (30 per family), four SOX-aligned approval tiers, six SoD constraints and eight role-entitlement mappings; ground truth for the 30 adversarial instances set by three domain experts with Cohen's kappa = 0.84
extraction.baseline: A conventional pre-deployment test suite of 47 unit tests and 18 scripted integration tests covering the same workflow steps, described as representative of current industry practice
extraction.key_results: Pre-deployment detection rate 89% (CDT) versus 43% (baseline), a 46 percentage-point gap, though the per-family table totals 134/150 = 89% versus 71/150 = 47%; SoD enforcement efficacy 96% versus 36%, with SoD false-negative rate 4% versus 64%; largest gaps on SoD and IAM boundary scenarios (97% versus 20%) and adversarial scenarios (80% versus 23%), smallest on routine flows (93% versus 83%); configuration-change detection latency 3.2 hours versus a simulated 14-day audit cycle; LLM judge ECE 0.041 (reduced from 0.068 after one recalibration), Brier score 0.172, chain-of-thought reasoning accuracy 0.83, judge-human agreement 86.7%.
extraction.limitations: Authors state the results come from a controlled simulation on a single synthetic workflow and are indicative rather than definitive; the agent behaviour model is probabilistic but scripted and does not capture production LLM agent outputs or their emergent failure modes; the baseline comparator is representative but simplified, so organizations with better test coverage may see higher baseline detection; generalization to larger agent ensembles and live regulatory data requires further study; cross-institutional and multi-jurisdictional settings are not addressed; the reliability model is correlational rather than causal; convergence guarantees for the autonomy policy under arbitrary distributional shift remain open.

title: Near-Miss: Latent Policy Failure Detection in Agentic Workflows
notes: This paper attacks a measurement assumption that RQ1 depends on: if policy adherence is scored by comparing the final system state against a gold state, agents that skip a mandatory verification step but still land on the right outcome are counted as compliant. The authors define a 'near-miss' or latent failure as a mutating tool call that was not adequately informed, operationalize it by replaying ToolGuard-generated guard code and searching the trajectory for the required read-only tool call or an information-equivalent substitute, and validate the detector against author annotation. Measured on six contemporary LLM agents, latent failures occur in 8-17% of trajectories containing mutating tool calls even when the final outcome matches ground truth, and the authors report that explicit policy violations account for roughly 25% of all simulation failures. For RQ1 this means outcome-only violation counts understate the true policy-violation rate, and any study comparing constrained against natural-language-instructed agents on final-state metrics alone will be biased in favour of the unconstrained agent. Note: the appendices reproduce the system prompts used for the detector; these are paper artifacts quoted as data and contain no instructions directed at this review.

quotes.text: Although not explicitly reported in prior work, our experiments suggest that policy violations account for approximately 25% of all simulation failures in theτ 2-bench Airlines domain
Both Claude-Sonnet4 and Kimi-K2.5 show near-miss rate (NMR) of 7% per human annotation.
Among the evaluated agents, GPT-oss-120b achieves the best result with a near-miss rate of 8.6%, followed by Claude-Sonnet4 with 12.1%.

extraction.framework: ToolGuard (the near-miss / latent-failure metric is built on top of it)
extraction.topology: single-agent ReAct-style tool-calling loop with a user simulator; ToolGuard guard code is replayed offline for evaluation rather than enforced at runtime
extraction.benchmark: tau2-verified Airlines domain (enhanced tau2-bench), 50 tasks with 4 trials each for 200 simulations per agent, GPT4.1 as user simulator; two data-access tools were added to the domain
extraction.baseline: Conventional reference-based evaluation that compares only the final database state against the expected gold state; the two history-search strategies (LLM-based search versus generated-code search) and six LLM agents are also compared against each other and against author-annotated near-miss ground truth
extraction.key_results: Latent failures occur in 8-17% of trajectories involving mutating tool calls even when the final outcome matches ground truth; per-model near-miss rate over trajectories with mutating tool calls: GPT-oss-120b 0.086, Qwen2.5-72b 0.084 (flagged as unreliable), Claude-Sonnet4 0.121, Gemini-3-pro 0.140, Kimi-K2.5 0.144, GPT5-chat 0.173; policy violations account for approximately 25% of all simulation failures; human-annotated near-miss rate was 7% for both Claude-Sonnet4 and Kimi-K2.5; generated-code search with Claude-Sonnet4 achieved precision 1.00 and recall 1.00 on both agents; no clear relationship emerged between the policy-violation ratio and the near-miss ratio; update_reservation_flights was the mutating tool most often invoked without checks and get_flight_status the most frequently bypassed read-only tool.
extraction.limitations: Authors state the approach is bounded by the quality of ToolGuard-generated guard code, since errors or omissions in the LLM-generated guards directly reduce detection accuracy; the pipeline adds computational overhead (extra LLM calls per trajectory and tool invocation for the LLM-based variant); ToolGuard is used only for offline evaluation rather than runtime enforcement; evaluation covers a single benchmark with a limited set of tools and policies, and the authors call for validation on additional domains and larger, more diverse settings; annotation was done by the authors rather than independent annotators.

title: From Business Events to Auditable Decisions: Ontology-Governed Graph Simulation for Enterprise AI
notes: LOM-action argues explicitly against the natural-language-instruction arm of RQ1: business scenario conditions injected as prompt instructions are treated by the model as soft preferences, so it may still act on the unrestricted graph. The proposed alternative binds the agent to a mandatory three-phase pipeline (scenario parsing, sandbox graph mutation, decision derivation on the evolved graph) with every mutation logged for auditor replay. The paper's most transferable contribution for RQ2 is a measurement idea: it separates answer accuracy from tool-chain F1 and defines an 'illusive accuracy' index as their difference, showing frontier baselines reaching about 80% accuracy while recording F1 of 0.00 on basic traversal tasks because they answered from parametric knowledge without ever touching the sandbox. On the scenario-constrained tasks, where the constrained graph genuinely differs from the static one, baseline accuracy also collapsed to 0.64-0.66 against 1.00. The comparison is confounded, which the authors concede: LOM-action is fine-tuned while the baselines are zero-shot, and the controlled ablation (same fine-tuning without the simulation curriculum) is not run.

quotes.text: LOM-action achieves 1.00 accuracy against 0.66 and 0.64 for the baselines—a 34-point gap attributable to Phase 2 bypass
Of 50 outputs: 47 produced correct binary answers with zero tool calls (pure natural language responses);
Allexperiments areconductedonsyntheticNeo4jsubgraphsof20–30nodes and 30–60 edges.

extraction.framework: LOM-action (Large Ontology Model with event-driven ontology simulation)
extraction.topology: single-agent dual-mode execution (skill mode for registered skill-ontology tool calls, reasoning mode for novel in-context computation) over an isolated graph_id-keyed sandbox, with a LOM-as-Judge step re-grounding outputs from delegated frontier models
extraction.benchmark: LOM-action benchmark: 11 function-calling tasks over a 19-function graph API suite on synthetic Neo4j subgraphs of 20-30 nodes and 30-60 edges, 200 training and 100 held-out test samples per task (2,200 train / 1,100 test) with disjoint graph UUIDs
extraction.baseline: Zero-shot frontier LLMs Doubao-1.8 and DeepSeek-V3.2 invoked through their native function-calling APIs with the full 19-function schema, means over three independent runs
extraction.key_results: Overall answer accuracy 93.82% (LOM-action) versus 80.00% (Doubao-1.8) and 80.18% (DeepSeek-V3.2); overall tool-chain F1 98.74% versus 24.42% and 36.21%; illusive accuracy index 0.56, 0.44 and -0.05 respectively; F1 = 0.00 for both baselines on all four basic traversal tasks despite near-perfect accuracy; on fc_constraint_connection accuracy 1.00 versus 0.66 and 0.64, a 34-point gap, with baseline F1 of 0.325 and 0.351; on the hybrid coloring task LOM-action F1 = 1.00 with accuracy 0.46; manual inspection of 50 Doubao-1.8 CONNECTIVITY outputs found 47 correct answers produced with zero tool calls and 3 malformed calls; LOM-action error mix: 47% in-context computation, 29% incomplete tool chain, 15% argument hallucination, 9% mode misclassification.
extraction.limitations: Authors state all experiments use synthetic Neo4j subgraphs of 20-30 nodes and 30-60 edges, far below real enterprise ontology scale, with no demonstration of cross-scale or cross-domain transfer; the fine-tuned versus zero-shot comparison does not isolate architectural contribution from training contribution and the controlled ablation (a Qwen3.5-27B fine-tuned without the Phase 2 simulation curriculum) has not been run; end-to-end latency, throughput and concurrent-event sandbox locking are unmeasured; scenario conditions are currently stated in event payload text rather than derived from ontology traversal; Task 11 is a graph-theoretic task whose enterprise connection is illustrative rather than grounded in a deployed process.

title: Provably Secure Agent Guardrail
notes: The ePCA framework refuses natural-language intent at the enforcement boundary: agents must serialize each action into a strongly typed payload that is deterministically compiled into first-order logic and checked by an SMT solver against hard-coded safety axioms, so unsafe transitions become UNSAT rather than blocked by judgement. For RQ2 the useful part is the head-to-head against the two control mechanisms practitioners actually deploy - stateless attribute-based access control and LLM-as-a-Judge - on a multi-step financial transfer task with time-segmentation and meta-rule attacks. ABAC failed by under-blocking because it evaluates steps in isolation, the LLM judge was unstable across models, and ePCA blocked all adversarial trajectories while accepting benign ones at 0.44 ms average verification latency versus roughly 15 seconds for the judge. The authors are unusually explicit that this is a mechanism demonstration rather than a statistical benchmark, and that the guarantee is only as complete as the hand-written axiom set, which is the key qualification for RQ1: it proves absence of violations of declared axioms, not absence of unsafe behaviour.

quotes.text: In the Multi-Step Financial Transfer task, the mechanism achieved a zero attack success rate and a zero false positive rate across state-of-the-art models.
For models that use LLM-as-the-Judge, the results are unstable.
Consequently, the verifier fundamentally proves the absence of violations against explicitly defined axioms, rather than the absence of unsafe behaviors.

extraction.topology: single untrusted LLM policy generator gated by a four-layer isolated verification plane (action proposal, deterministic translation, SMT formal verification, deterministic checking) acting as a reference monitor over the tool interface
extraction.benchmark: No public benchmark; two constructed environments - Scenario A, a controlled multi-step financial transfer task with time-segmentation and meta-rule attacks plus benign sequences, and Scenario B, an enterprise sandbox with a dual-zone network topology and five axioms, exercised through a 12-round data-exfiltration trajectory
extraction.baseline: Stateless Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) and empirical semantic guardrails implemented as LLM-as-a-Judge, both run across the same front-end models (GPT-5.2, GPT-5.4, Claude-Sonnet 4.6, Qwen3-Max, Gemini 3.1 Flash, Kimi k2.5)
extraction.key_results: In Scenario A, ePCA reached 100.0% accuracy, 0.0% false-alarm rate and 100.0% F1 for every evaluated model; ABAC reached 50.0% accuracy / 66.7% F1 for four of five models and 98.3% / 99.2% for Gemini-3-flash; LLM-as-a-Judge ranged from 43.3% to 100.0% accuracy and 60.5% to 100.0% F1, with Claude-Sonnet 4.6 producing no valid executions; average decision latency 0.44 ms for ePCA versus 1.52e4 ms for the LLM judge and 1.10e-3 ms for ABAC. In Scenario B the 12-round exfiltration attempt was blocked by taint-lock axioms and the agent self-terminated after recognizing the deadlock.
extraction.limitations: Authors state the architecture relies on strongly typed schemas and static syntactic parsing, leaving it exposed to advanced schema-evasion attacks, while adding a neural parser would reintroduce probabilistic uncertainty; finite formal constraints cannot cover open, high-degree-of-freedom action spaces, so only critical operational paths are constrained; the axiom set is hard-coded from human expert modelling and scales poorly to multi-agent tasks with large dynamic state spaces; most fundamentally, the verifier proves absence of violations of explicitly defined axioms rather than absence of unsafe behaviour, so an omitted constraint yields a mathematically compliant but unsafe transition; empirical conclusions are limited to micro-benchmarking in controlled environments and the authors describe the experiments as illustrative realizations rather than statistically representative benchmarks; open, multi-tool and heterogeneous multi-agent evaluation is left to future work.

title: SARC: A Governance-by-Architecture Framework for Agentic AI Systems
notes: SARC adds an explicit constraint primitive to the reinforcement-learning tuple and compiles each constraint declaration into one of four enforcement sites in the agent loop, with placement determined by constraint class (hard before dispatch, soft over completed actions, escalation through a router bounded by the action's reversibility window). For RQ1 the paper supplies both an argument and a caveat: it argues that prompt-layer guardrails cannot enforce hard constraints by construction because the model can route around them through tools whose effects are off-screen, and it proves that finite additive reward penalties cannot substitute for hard constraints when violations are low-probability and high-payoff. For RQ2 it runs a controlled comparison of five governance regimes over 50 seeds, and is notably careful about attribution - the 89.5% reduction in soft-window overages is credited to the declared throttling response being placed at the post-action auditor, not to the SARC label, and the authors state a policy-as-code system with the same response would perform similarly. The critical limitation for evidence quality is that the agent is a simulated procurement policy, not an LLM, so the results measure enforcement architecture rather than agent behaviour under instruction.

quotes.text: Prompt guardrails cannot enforce hard constraints by construction because the model may ignore, reinterpret, or route around them through tools whose effects are off-screen.
SARC reduces soft-window overages from ∼937 (policy-as-code-only) to98.8± 1.0, a89.5%reduction at95%confidence.

First, the environment is synthetic and intentionally stylized; results from a synthetic procurement task do not generalize to real procurement, customer-service, or clinical settings without further empirical work.

extraction.topology: single-agent loop with four enforcement points (Pre-Action Gate, Action-Time Monitor, Post-Action Auditor, Escalation Router); a multi-agent extension defines constraint inheritance, authority intersection along orchestrator-worker call chains, and attribution-preserving trace trees
extraction.benchmark: No public benchmark; a synthetic procurement environment with 1,000 orders per episode over 50 random seeds, log-normal order amounts, one hard constraint (approval above EUR 50,000), one soft constraint (rolling 24-hour spend at or above EUR 475,000) and one escalation constraint (first-time supplier review), with a deliberately misaligned reward; artifacts released at github.com/besanson/sarc-governance
extraction.baseline: Four practitioner regimes: post-hoc audit, output filtering (modelled at 25% post-action coverage of the hard constraint), workflow rules (if/else gate before tool dispatch), and policy-as-code-only (hard constraint at the policy layer, escalation at the pre-action gate, no declared post-action throttling response)
extraction.key_results: Executed hard-constraint violations per episode (mean, 95% CI): post-hoc audit 26.8 +/- 1.4, output filter 19.4 +/- 1.1, workflow rules 0.0, policy-as-code-only 0.0, SARC 0.0; soft-window overages 949.8, 947.4, 935.6, 937.1 and 98.8 +/- 1.0 respectively, an 89.5% reduction versus policy-as-code-only; suppliers cleared without review 132.3, 132.7, 129.0, 0.0 and 0.0; escalations 0, 0, 0, 133.8 +/- 2.5 and 160.2 +/- 3.3; per-step latency 0, 0.07, 12, 15 and 21 ms. Under a predicate-noise sweep, residual SARC violations rose from 0.00 at zero error to 3.66 +/- 0.59 per episode at predicate false-negative rate 0.10 and enforcement failure rate 0.05. The audit checker reported zero structural discrepancies across all 50 SARC seeds.
extraction.limitations: Authors state three threats to validity: the environment is synthetic and stylized and does not generalize to real procurement, customer-service or clinical settings; per-step latency figures are model parameters of each regime rather than measurements of any implementation; the reward is deliberately misaligned to expose the enforcement gap, and under a well-aligned reward the gap may narrow. They also state the evaluation does not show that SARC outperforms safe-RL training and includes no adversarial or indirect-prompt-injection testing; the zero-violation curve assumes exact predicates, active enforcement at every step and no bypass paths; the framework does not solve legal interpretation, predicate correctness, model reliability or organizational accountability; and state-dependent recursive call depth and out-of-trust-boundary market topologies in multi-agent settings are not formally characterized.
